questions.q: What are the three main components of setting in a narrative, and which component is most prominently established in the opening paragraph of "igyoku dh <ksyd"?
questions.a: The three main components are time (historical period, time of day), place (geographical location, physical environment), and social environment (cultural norms, power structures). The opening paragraph establishes place most prominently, describing the village with its bell tower, dusty lanes, river, and fields. A wrong answer that only says "village" without breaking down the components shows the student cannot distinguish between the elements of setting.

questions.q: Explain in your own words how the sound of the bell (igyoku dh <ksyd) functions as both a setting detail and an atmosphere builder in the story.
questions.a: The bell is a physical object in the village (place), marking time (temporal setting), and represents British authority (social setting). Its regular clang — "pV~&èkk, fxM+&èkk" — creates an atmosphere of control and monotony; when it stops or changes rhythm, the atmosphere shifts to tension or freedom. A wrong answer that treats the bell only as a plot device (e.g., "it tells people when to work") misses its dual role in establishing setting and evoking mood.

questions.q: Compare the atmosphere of the village during the daily bell routine with the atmosphere after the bell stops ringing permanently. What does this shift reveal about the relationship between setting and power?
questions.a: During the routine, the atmosphere is oppressive, mechanical, and fearful — the bell dictates life. After it stops, the atmosphere becomes uncertain but alive with human voices and natural sounds, showing that the colonial power structure (embodied in the bell) has been broken. A wrong answer that only describes the two atmospheres without linking the shift to power dynamics fails to analyze the deeper connection.

questions.q: Evaluate the author's choice to set the climax during a violent storm. Is the storm merely a dramatic backdrop, or does it serve a deeper thematic purpose? Justify your view with evidence.
questions.a: The storm is not just backdrop; it mirrors the internal turmoil of Yashwant and the villagers, and its destruction of the bell tower symbolizes the shattering of colonial control. The lightning striking the tower is nature's verdict on an unjust system. A wrong answer that calls it "just weather for drama" ignores the symbolic layer the author builds through setting.

questions.q: Write a short paragraph (4-5 sentences) describing the village market scene from the perspective of a child who has never heard the bell stop, using at least three sensory details from the text to create a vivid atmosphere.
questions.a: A strong answer will include sensory details like the smell of rain on dust, the sound of vendors' cries mixing with the bell, the sight of colorful cloth and vegetables, the feel of mud underfoot, and convey the child's wonder or fear. A weak answer lists details without weaving them into a coherent atmosphere or perspective.
